lines.text: What happens if you drink a slushie way too fast?
Well, your throat gets freezing cold in seconds,
so the blood vessels there tighten, then snap wide open.
That rush of blood sets off pain nerves,
and your brain feels it in your forehead.
It fades in seconds, and it can't hurt you.

sources: Britannica, 'What Causes Brain Freeze?' (rapid cooling of the roof of the mouth or back of the throat; blood vessels constrict, then rebound dilate; trigeminal nerve carries the signal; brain misinterprets it as forehead pain — referred pain; lasts only seconds to a few minutes)

Science Times, 'From Ice Cream to Instant Headache: The Physiology Behind Brain Freeze' (vasoconstriction followed by vasodilation; the rapid shift in blood flow creates pressure changes that stimulate nearby nerves; trigeminal nerve; referred pain)

Mental Floss, 'Why Do People Get Ice Cream Headaches?' (rapid cooling makes vessels constrict, then rebound dilation; pain receptors send signals via the trigeminal nerve; the brain interprets them as coming from the forehead)
Harvard-affiliated 2012 study (Serrador et al., FASEB Journal): blood flow through the anterior cerebral artery surged as volunteers signalled brain-freeze pain, then faded as the pain faded
title: What Happens If You Drink a Slushie Too Fast?
